title: Binary and hex for network engineers

cards.heading: Eight bits, eight place values
cards.body: Every IPv4 octet is 8 bits. From left to right the bits are worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. A bit set to 1 adds its value; a 0 adds nothing. The largest octet, all ones, is 255.

cards.heading: Decimal to binary
cards.body: Walk the place values left to right. If the value fits in what is left, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0. Stop when nothing is left and fill the rest with zeros.
cards.example:
200: 128 fits (72 left), 64 fits (8 left), 32 no, 16 no,
     8 fits (0 left), 4 no, 2 no, 1 no
200 = 1100 1000

cards.heading: The mask values to memorise
cards.body: Subnet mask octets are always ones followed by zeros, so only nine values are possible. Each one adds the next place value to the previous. Knowing these by heart is what makes subnetting fast. Count the 1 bits to get the prefix length: in the last octet 128 is /25, 192 /26, 224 /27, 240 /28, 248 /29, 252 /30 (add 24 for the first three 255 octets).
cards.mnemonic:
Start at 128 and keep adding half of what you just added: 128, +64 = 192, +32 = 224, +16 = 240, +8 = 248, +4 = 252, +2 = 254, +1 = 255.
Or work back from the block size: mask = 256 - block. A block of 64 gives 192, a block of 4 gives 252.
Easy to mix up: 252 is /30 (the two-host link mask) and 254 is /31.

cards.heading: Hex in one step
cards.body: Split the byte into two 4-bit halves (nibbles). Each nibble is one hex digit from 0 to F, where A=10 through F=15. You will see hex in MAC addresses and in every IPv6 address. To go back to decimal, the left hex digit is worth 16s and the right one 1s: 0xAC = 10 x 16 + 12 = 172.
